The model implementation is not supplied. Diagnosis relies on the SASRec compatibility interface: `item_emb.weight`, `log2feats(sequence)`, and `predict_score(features, items)`. It computes sequence features for every position and scores paired positive/negative items. The internal representation computation and final-user-feature selection cannot be verified from this code; this probe evaluates valid training positions rather than explicitly selecting a final user representation.

# Diagnosis Inputs & Hooks

`DiagnosisProbe(model, device)` stores the model/view and its `meta_data`, `review_data`, and `user_train`; only metadata is subsequently used. `run_full_diagnosis(train_loader)` invokes two probes. Margin analysis switches the model to evaluation mode and processes up to ten batches containing `(None, sequence, positive, negative)`. Positive ID zero marks padding and is excluded. Both probes disable gradients.

# Probes & Metrics

- **`embedding_collapse_score`**: Samples at most 2,048 nonpadding item embeddings using seed 42, normalizes them, averages off-diagonal pairwise cosine similarities, and maps the result through `(cosine + 1)/2`. Higher values suggest directional collapse; approximately 0.5 indicates zero mean cosine, not necessarily poor health.
- **`pos_neg_margin_mean` / `pos_neg_margin_p10`**: Mean and empirical tenth percentile of positive minus negative logits. Higher values indicate stronger separation, including among difficult positions.
- **`pos_neg_neg_beats_pos_rate`**: Fraction with negative margin; lower is better.
- **`pos_neg_small_margin_rate`**: Fraction with margin below 0.5; lower indicates fewer weakly separated pairs.
- **`pos_neg_margin_category_breakdown`**: Counts category occurrences separately for positive and negative items in low-margin and wrong-ranking cases, retaining the top 20 categories.

No sequence shuffling, deletion, substitution, or sensitivity tests occur. Random embedding subsampling reduces computation; supplied negatives test pairwise score separation.

 ## Search results
Recent research identifies distinct popularity and recency failure modes. [Lin et al. (2024/2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12008) locate popularity in the principal spectrum of predicted scores and link its amplification to dimension collapse. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) measure excessive dependence on recent interactions and report improvements from mitigation. Diagnostic implication: measure personalization beyond a popularity baseline and separate sensitivity to recent versus older history; recommendation stability alone cannot establish usefulness.

[Zhang and Nanda (ICLR 2024)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/06a52a54c8ee03cd86771136bc91eb1f-Abstract-Conference.html) show that activation-patching conclusions depend strongly on corruption methods and evaluation metrics. Proposed transfer to recommenders: pair histories within dataset, matching length, item-popularity distribution and temporal characteristics; separately shuffle order, replace recent items and exchange older histories. Ablate encoder, recent-history branch and scoring contributions, then patch clean activations into matched corrupted runs. Report target-score margins, target ranks and validation HR@10 changes alongside list overlap. These interventions diagnose model computation, not causal effects on users’ preferences.

[Zaman and Srivastava (EMNLP 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18848) validate faithfulness metrics against deliberately constructed faithful/unfaithful pairs; diagnosticity varies across tasks and models. Suggested controls: a history-independent popularity scorer should show zero history sensitivity; a synthetic last-item scorer should respond specifically to last-item replacement; identity patches should reproduce baseline outputs. For DiagnosisProbe, use fixed samples/candidates, evaluation mode and inference-only execution; restore RNG states, module modes and hooks afterward, and verify unchanged parameters/buffers. Label these engineering adaptations explicitly; the cited work does not establish a validated sequential-recommender probe suite.

Recent work distinguishes factual grounding from model faithfulness: an explanation can match metadata yet misrepresent what influenced ranking. The [2024 faithfulness survey](https://aclanthology.org/2024.cl-2.6/) supports intervention-based evaluation; [2025 counterfactual research](https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/walk-the-talk-llm-faithfulness/) tests whether claimed influential concepts actually change predictions. For this task, proposed probes should remove cited history items and measure score/rank changes, comparing against matched random removals. These are sensitivity diagnostics, not proof of user intent. Validate perceived specificity against explicit feedback only where available; otherwise report it as unmeasured.

A practical approach without pretrained models: fit word/character TF-IDF on training-item titles/descriptions, freeze vocabulary/IDF, and compare candidates with individual history items and aggregated profiles. [Scikit-learn documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.0/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.html) supports this sparse representation. Proposed diagnostics: rare-term overlap, specific-interest coverage, and broad-match outranking of specific matches. Extract explicit model identifiers, connectors, dimensions and voltage using rules, retaining source spans and normalized units. Assign supported, contradicted or unknown status; missing specifications require abstention from compatibility claims, not an incompatibility label.

Complementarity, substitution and redundancy need separate evidence. [Amazon’s complementary-recommendation research](https://www.amazon.science/blog/improving-complementary-product-recommendations) emphasizes directional relationships and overlapping behavioral signals: co-occurrence alone cannot establish compatibility or complementarity. Here, interaction association and lexical similarity should remain provisional indicators. Report near-duplicate recommendations as potential redundancy, never as proof that a need is already satisfied. Histories do not establish ownership, equipment availability or latent diversity/conformity traits. Keep these diagnostics separate from the required macro validation HR@10 selection metric.

Sampled evaluation can reverse model rankings relative to full-catalog evaluation. A direct sequential-recommendation study found inconsistencies with both uniform and popularity-weighted samples, including commonly used 100-item candidate sets ([Dallmann et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13045)). RecSys 2025 examined sampling fidelity, robustness and predictive power, reinforcing that candidate selection affects conclusions ([On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). Separately, a 2024 sequential-recommendation study comparing training samplers found aggregate accuracy concealed head/mid/tail disparities; random sampling favored head items, while popularity-based methods traded overall performance for more balanced results ([Prakash et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). Popularity-weighted sampling is therefore a useful stress test, without guaranteeing agreement with full-catalog rankings.

Practical synthesis: replace raw score-margin probes with a separate training-history ranking audit. Use observed prefix→next-item examples; exclude prefix-seen items while retaining the target. Compare target rank and HR@10 across repeated unique uniform negatives, negatives matched to the target’s training-frequency band, model-scored hard negatives, and the complete eligible catalog. Report target-rank percentiles, hit/miss disagreement, and model-order disagreement across protocols; stratify by history length and target popularity. Bootstrap users with paired resampling across protocols, retaining all examples from each user together; report candidate-resampling variability separately.
